newsitem.title: NORWAY: E.Timor activists win Peace Prize, Indonesia fumes.
newsitem.headline: E.Timor activists win Peace Prize, Indonesia fumes.

text.p: Two East Timor independence campaigners were awarded the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize on Friday in a decision that angered the territory's ruler, Indonesia, but won global praise.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee, sharply criticising Indonesia which invaded the territory in 1975, said the award to East Timor Bishop Carlos Belo and resistance leader Jose Ramos-Horta aimed to influence the drawn-out conflict there.

The prestigious award, which confirmed the committee's ability to stir controversy, was welcomed by the United Nations, former colonial power Portugal, the Vatican, Amnesty International, the European Union and the United States.
Committee chairman Francis Sejersted told reporters at the Nobel Institute in Oslo. "This was about to become a forgotten conflict and we wanted to contribute to maintaining the momentum."
"We do hope there is a message (in this award)...to the Indonesian government to change its policy."
The United States said it hoped the award would help efforts to settle problems in the Indonesian-ruled territory.

Indonesia condemned the award. The country's foreign minister Ali Alatas said he was "astounded" Ramos-Horta had won, calling him a "political adventurist". He did not comment on Belo, 50, East Timor's outspoken and often fiery Roman Catholic bishop.
"All I can say is that I'm quite astounded at the choice of the Nobel commitee," Alatas said, adding Ramos-Hortha could not be compared to previous winners of the prestigious prize.
East Timor has bedevilled Indonesia's international relations since it invaded the territory in December 1975 and formally annexed it in July 1976.
The United Nations does not recognise Indonesian rule in East Timor, which lies about 500 kms (300 miles) north of Australia, and regards former colonial ruler Portugal as the administering power.

"In the years that followed (the invasion) it has been estimated a third of East Timor's population lost their lives due to starvation, epidemics, war and terror," the Nobel committee said, publicly accusing Indonesia of oppression.
The U.N. has brokered regular meetings between Indonesia and Portugal and started an intra-Timorese dialogue but progress has been painfully slow. The next meeting is due in December.
U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali said he hoped the award would "positively affect the continuing negotiations in the search for a lasting settlement".
Portugal reacted with delight, saying it could push Indonesia into easing its iron grip over the territory.
But diplomatic and political analysts said it would be hard for the Indonesian government to swallow the decision and could even delay peace efforts.

"In a sense it represents the acknowledgement of the international community that Indonesia's claims to successful integration (of East Timor) haven't been accepted," a diplomatic source in Indonesia told Reuters.
Amnesty International, the human rights watchdog, welcomed the award but said the international community needed to watch developments now to ensure there was no new crackdown.
"The human rights situation in East Timor remains extremely grave," Amnesty said in a statement.
Belo, who was saying mass in a school in the East Timor capital Dili when the $1.12 million award was announced, spoke of peace and reconciliation.
"I see it as a victory for East Timorese...and all Indonesians," he told Reuters. "Peace can be achieved through non-violent means."
The reaction from Ramos-Horta, a U.S. educated lawyer who fled to Australia three days before the invasion, was mixed.

"I'm happy but surprised, because Bishop Belo deserves the Nobel Peace Prize but the other person who should be sharing the award with him is my leader, Xanana Gusmao," Ramos-Horta told Reuters from his mother's home in Sydney, Australia.
Gusmao is serving a 20-year jail sentence in Indonesia.
